newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-SLAMS WILL BE LESS GRAND WITHOUT EDBERG.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SLAMS WILL BE LESS GRAND WITHOUT EDBERG.

text.p: The Grand Slam landscape was a little less grand on Friday with the departure from the scene of Stefan Edberg.
With a quarter-final loss to Goran Ivanisevic at the U.S. Open, the final chapter was written of a distinguished Grand Slam career, which began 13 years ago at Wimbledon.
The smooth Swede decided last year, with his game in decline, that he was ready to give up the peripatetic tennis life at 30.

His 14th U.S. Open was to be his Grand Slam swan song and the melody was provided by a cheering chorus of thousands, crooning appreciation for what he's accomplished and inspiring him to play on a little longer.
Always a gentleman, Edberg was not excitable enough to suit some people. But style, class, grace and elegance are also held in esteem, and Edberg personifies those attributes.
The sportsmanship, civility and modesty he presented on and off court are all too rare in the world of big-money, big-ego professional sports.
And while his strokes may lack the explosiveness in vogue with today's power-hitters, his game was a thing of beauty.
The grace with which Edberg moved from serve to volley conjured up images of Fred Astaire without the top hat. And his backhand volley was simply the prettiest shot in the tennis world.

The Open was the 20th stop on Edberg's farewell tour. But warm receptions all along the way were tempered by inconsistent and disappointing results that seemed to confirm his decision to call it a day.
In January, he said G'day to the Australian Open -- where he had his first taste of Grand Slam glory -- in the second round.
Edberg won Australian titles in 1985 and 1987 and was a finalist three times more in the '90s.
In May, he bid adieu to Roland Garros -- the one that got away -- with a fourth-round exit after a rejuvenating win over American Michael Chang.

Edberg came close there only once in 1989, making the final. But the French Open script that year called for a miracle win by a gutsy 17-year-old who came from nowhere -- Chang, who would later figure in some of the Swede's happier memories.

It was obvious from early on that Edberg had the game to win on Wimbledon grass. And for three successive years -- from 1988 to 1990 -- he and Boris Becker battled it out on the final Sunday with the elegant Swede twice prevailing.
But the U.S. Open was Connors, McEnroe and Lendl country. You had to be either a madman or a machine to thrive in New York.
Edberg appeared just too nice to win the U.S. Open. And his early Flushing experiences were mostly a series of forgettable days and regrettable nights.
Bothered by the myriad discomforts and distractions that make the Open more a survival test than a tennis tournament, Edberg often appeared ill at ease on the green concrete.
That all changed with a pair of magnificent back-to-back Open runs that forever altered the way Edberg's career will be remembered.
In the fourth round in 1991 it was Chang who forced Edberg to raise his game and the Swede took it to a level rarely seen before or since.
For the next three matches, Edberg was poetry and perfection, making it look almost too easy.
"I probably played the best match of my life on that court when I beat (Jim) Courier in the '91 final," he recalled.

But it was his 1992 title defence that proved to his detractors, and to Edberg himself, that he had the heart of a champion -- the ability to get up off the canvas and score a knockout when things looked bleak.
Edberg came back from down a break in the fifth set against Richard Krajicek in the fourth round, Ivan Lendl in the quarters, and Chang in the semifinal.

They seemed to hit a million shots that sunny Saturday when he and Chang battled for nearly five-and-a-half hours -- the longest U.S. Open match on record. And still Edberg had enough left to beat Pete Sampras in the final.

"The most special year was '92, the way that I won it, being down all the time and playing all these five setters," Edberg said. "That's probably tennis-wise the biggest achievement of my career. That's a vintage year."

His typical Swedish reserve often concealed the depth of Edberg's competitive nature. But his reason for quitting when he could surely play on for several more years, unmasks the fire beneath the ice.
When he felt the major titles that most players only dream of but never get near were beyond his grasp, it was time to ride off into the sunset.
It was never about celebrity or a big payday for Edberg, it was about competing at the highest level -- and winning.
So after a record 54 consecutive Grand Slam appearances, six major titles and a 178-47 major match record, the softly-spoken Swede wrote his own tennis epitaph.
"I want to be remembered as a champion and a sportsman."
He can rest easy on both counts.
